title: Review a React effect that creates a subscription leak
description: Problem: Review a React effect that creates a subscription leak. Solve this problem with multiple approaches and detailed explanations.

data.text: **Review a React effect that creates a subscription leak** is a memory-management bug. When a useEffect subscribes to an event source, timer, or WebSocket and does not return a cleanup function, the subscription outlives the component. The callback continues to fire after unmount, holding a closure over stale state and preventing garbage collection. In a long-lived SPA with frequent navigation, leaked subscriptions accumulate and eventually crash the tab.
What leaks in a React effect

items: setInterval and setTimeout callbacks that are never cleared
addEventListener calls to window, document, or DOM elements without matching removeEventListener
WebSocket and EventSource connections left open after unmount
RxJS subscriptions not unsubscribed in the cleanup return
Firebase listeners, Pusher channels, and SSE connections that are never disconnected
requestAnimationFrame loops that keep running after the component is gone

terms.definition: An event listener, timer, or connection that continues to fire after the subscribing component unmounts.
The function returned from useEffect that runs before unmount and before the next effect invocation.
A function that captures variables from its outer scope. If the function outlives the component, the captured variables stay in memory.
A DOM element removed from the document but still referenced by JavaScript, preventing garbage collection.
React 18+ development mode that double-invokes effects to surface missing cleanup functions.

data.text: The leak happens in three steps. First, the effect subscribes to something external. Second, the component unmounts because the user navigates away. Third, the subscription continues to fire because there is no cleanup. Each callback closes over the component's state and setState, so even though the component is gone, the closure keeps it alive.

data.title: Leak: interval not cleared on unmount
data.content: The component sets an interval but never clears it. After unmount, the interval fires forever, each callback closing over the stale setPrice reference:

data.title: Fix: always return a cleanup function
data.content: The cleanup function runs before unmount and before the next effect run, breaking the reference:

data.title: Rules for useEffect cleanup
items: If the effect subscribes to anything, it must return a cleanup function that unsubscribes
If the effect uses addEventListener, the cleanup must call removeEventListener with the same handler reference
If the effect starts a WebSocket, the cleanup must call .close()
If the effect starts an RxJS subscription, the cleanup must call .unsubscribe()
If the effect uses requestAnimationFrame, the cleanup must call cancelAnimationFrame
The cleanup function is also called before the next effect run when dependencies change

data.caption: Effect lifecycle with and without cleanup
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Component mounts] --> B[useEffect fires]
    B --> C[Subscribe: interval / event / socket]
    C --> D{Component unmounts?}
    D -->|Yes| E{Cleanup returned?}
    E -->|Yes| F[Unsubscribe: clear / remove / close]
    E -->|No| G[Subscription continues firing]
    G --> H[Closure holds component state]
    H --> I[Component cannot be garbage collected]
    F --> J[Memory freed]
    D -->|No| K[Component continues]
    K --> L{Dependencies change?}
    L -->|Yes| M[Cleanup runs, then effect re-runs]
    M --> C

data.text: React 18 Strict Mode as a safety net

React 18 Strict Mode double-invokes effects in development. If your cleanup is missing, you will see duplicate intervals or subscriptions immediately. This is not a bug in React; it is a feature designed to expose leaks before they reach production. Always develop with Strict Mode enabled and treat duplicate-effect warnings as real defects.

data.title: The fetch-in-interval trap
data.text: A fetch inside setInterval that uses a stale closure is especially dangerous. Each callback captures the setPrice from the render when the interval was created. After unmount, the interval keeps firing and each call allocates a Promise. In a long-lived SPA, mount and unmount happen repeatedly, multiplying the leak.

items: Use the Performance API with memory (Chrome-only) to log usedJSHeapSize on a schedule
Alert when usedJSHeapSize grows past a threshold without plateauing
Compare heap snapshots in Chrome DevTools before and after navigating away from a suspect page
Look for 'Detached HTMLDivElement' or 'closure' entries that grew significantly
Trace retainers back to your code to find the effect keeping them alive

items.text: Every addEventListener has a matching removeEventListener in the cleanup return
items.hint: Use the same handler reference—do not define the handler inline

items.text: Every setInterval / setTimeout is cleared in cleanup
items.hint: Store the ID in a ref if the callback references changing state

items.text: WebSocket and EventSource are closed in cleanup
items.hint: Check for .close() calls in the return function
Use takeUntil with a Subject for RxJS; call unsubscribe() for Firebase

items.text: Large objects in closures are not captured unnecessarily
items.hint: If the interval only needs a small value, extract just that value into the closure

data.title: Fix subscription leaks
data.description: Open a project with multiple useEffect hooks. Audit each one for missing cleanup functions. Add cleanup, then verify with Strict Mode and Chrome DevTools heap snapshots.
steps: Search the codebase for useEffect without a return statement
For each, identify whether it subscribes to an external source
Add the matching cleanup: clearInterval, removeEventListener, close, or unsubscribe
Run the app in Strict Mode and confirm no duplicate effects appear
Take a heap snapshot before and after navigating to and from the page
data.expectedOutcome: No detached DOM nodes or retained closures should remain after navigating away from the page.

items.question: Can React itself leak memory?
items.answer: React is careful with memory. Leaks almost always come from developer-written effects, third-party libraries holding references, or closures capturing more than needed. React 19's use() and useEffect Event patterns reduce the leak surface.

items.question: What is a WeakRef and when would I use it?
items.answer: WeakRef holds a weak reference to an object so it does not prevent garbage collection. You would use it for a cache where you want entries to expire automatically. Most React leaks are better fixed by removing the strong reference entirely.

items.question: How do I find a leak without DevTools in production?
items.answer: Log usedJSHeapSize from the Performance API on a timer. Alert when it grows past a threshold and correlate with user actions. Pair with server-side error tracking to catch crashes caused by memory pressure.

data.title: Summary
points: Every useEffect that subscribes to something external must return a cleanup function
Strict Mode double-invoking effects is your friend—it catches leaks in development
Use heap snapshots to find detached DOM nodes and retained closures
Clear intervals, remove listeners, close sockets, and unsubscribe in cleanup
Avoid capturing large objects in closures that outlive the component
data.takeaway: Memory leaks in React are effect-management bugs. The fix is always the same: clean up.
